judgements.reason: Same mechanism (LLM-controlled `host`/`proxy` tool args spread into the options object via `{ ...args, managementToken }` in exportSpace.ts/importSpace.ts), same sink (contentful-export/import -> CMA client baseURL), and same consequence (the server's CMA PAT is sent to an attacker-chosen endpoint). It also names the same file and the same line ranges as the advisory.

Same file and same root pattern (caller args spread into the authenticated request options), but a different parameter and a different effect: `headers` (header override / non-string header values), not `host`/`proxy`. The advisory's defining consequence is the PAT being redirected to an attacker host via baseURL; header injection is an adjacent abuse of the same merge, not that defect.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: If the advisory had enumerated `headers` among the LLM-controlled transport options it considers part of the flaw, this would be a subset of the same defect; it names only `host` and `proxy`.

judgements.reason: Same file (exportSpace.ts) and same trust-boundary class, but a different defect: caller-controlled `exportDir`/`contentFile`/`errorLogFile` produce arbitrary local file write and path traversal. No credential leaves the host and no request is redirected, so neither the mechanism nor the consequence in the advisory is reproduced.

Same file (importSpace.ts) and same class of unfiltered tool arguments, but a different defect: read-side path arguments (`contentFile`, `assetsDirectory`, `config`) give local file disclosure and exfiltration as CMS assets. The sink is the filesystem and the destination space, not the `host`-derived baseURL that carries the PAT.

Same files and the same `{ ...args, managementToken }` merge, but a different parameter and effect: `spaceId`/`environmentId` override the operator-configured scope, so the token acts on unintended spaces. The credential stays with Contentful; it is not redirected off-box, which is the advisory's defect.

Adjacent, not the same: it concerns the registration/gating of the very tools the advisory covers (register.ts disable/enable latching), a defence-in-depth exposure-window issue that the finding itself frames as lowering the cost of F-001 rather than being the flaw. Different file, different mechanism, no credential redirection.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: It sits on the boundary between `partial` and `no`; I kept `partial` only because it is scoped to exportSpace/importSpace, the exact component the advisory is about.

judgements.reason: Same file and same function (getHTMLFromAtext in src/node/utils/ExportHtml.ts) and the same attacker-controlled source (a pad line attribute from the pool), but a different defect: an unbounded list-level loop causing heap exhaustion/DoS, not unescaped interpolation of attribute values into `span data-<k>="<v>"` yielding stored XSS. Different mechanism, different consequence, different lines (351/465 vs the data-attribute emission).
Version/build fingerprint disclosure through getPublicSettings() in Settings.ts. Different file, different mechanism, different effect; nothing to do with HTML-attribute escaping in the exporter.

SESSIONKEY.txt written without a restrictive mode in Settings.ts — a local file-permission issue on the session signing key. Unrelated to the export-path XSS; it is also not the advisory's secondary note, which is about default/placeholder account and SSO credentials being configured.

The `x-proxy-path` header being honoured regardless of trustProxy, in Settings.ts. Different file, different input channel (request header vs pad attribute pool) and different effect (URL-prefix control / cache poisoning), not the unescaped export attribute.
Missing requireTLS in the SMTP settings shape in Settings.ts — cleartext AUTH to a mail relay. No overlap in file, mechanism or effect with the HTML-export XSS.
